newsitem.title: USA: Folgers U.S. retail coffee prices unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Folgers U.S. retail coffee prices unchanged.

text.p: Major U.S. coffee roaster Folgers Coffee Co, a division of Proctor and Gamble said it had no immediate plans to raise retail prices in the U.S. despite rocketing futures prices.
However, Folgers added it would continue to monitor the market closely.
"We do not have news of a price increase," a Folgers spokeswoman said. "Like everyone else we watch the market to see if there is a sustainable price."
Earlier this week, Procter and Gamble's Canadian division said it will raise the price of Folgers coffee in Canada on Feb 1 to reflect gains in green bean prices.

"Our intention is to reflect North American green bean prices," said a spokeswoman for Proctor's Canadian unit. "We last lowered the price on Aug 1, and that was to be in line with competitive pricing."
Coffee prices on Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York have surged 20 percent since the end of 1996 as U.S. consumer coffee inventories hovered at low levels.
Despite dwindling stockpiles and the sharp rise in futures, traders said U.S. roasters were likely hold retail prices steady until the market's bull run subsided.
"The worst thing the roasters can do is announce a price increase," a physical coffee trader said. "They do not want to fuel the fire."

Traders said the tight supply situation caught many roasters by surprise. Normally, an increased flow of new crop coffee from Latin America during the first quarter builds stockpiles, but aggressive purchasing by European roasters has absorbed some of the new crop supply.
Stocks of coffee certified against the CSCE were at extremely low, standing at 22,102 60-kg bags as of Jan. 22, the CSCE reported.
Green Coffee Association of New York reported last week, U.S. consumer coffee stocks rose by 63,000 bags in December, but were still at low levels at 1,327,000 bags.
Physical traders said tight supply concerns could escalate if top-grower Brazil's 1997/98 crop were to come in smaller than this season's harvest as many industry sources fear.

Preliminary forecasts by the Brazilian government have pegged the country's 1997/98 coffee crop between 18 million and 20 million 60-kg bags compared with an estimated 25 million bags the previous season. ((--Patricia Avidan, New York Commodities Desk, 212 859 1640))
